prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I move from the Higgs experiments (B005) to optical lattice clocks. The decisive step that separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is a physical idea, not a better number: at the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held without perturbing the transition. That changes the statistics, since the signal grows with the atom number, and it puts the clock in a regime where the interesting physics is the systematic effect itself. Combs made optical frequencies countable and ions showed single-particle control; neither contained this idea. The result has been checked against rival devices in Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE at the 10^-18 level, and it now delivers clues from nature rather than elegant arguments: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body and spin-exchange effects inside the clock, bounds on varying constants and on dark-matter couplings. A citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice expresses this and cannot be read as a second comb prize. The credit is compact: Katori proposed the scheme and made the first demonstrations, and Ye took it to the accuracy, stability and many-body frontier. Members from atomic physics, instrumentation, condensed matter and statistical physics reach this independently, and that spread of expertise counts for more with me than the number of first places.
statement.case_against: The honest objection is novelty and character: this is metrology, and a sceptic can call it a superb refinement of an optical-frequency-standards lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012. The fundamental return, the redshift tests, constant variation and dark-matter searches, is still largely prospective, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the committee could wait. Priority at the margin (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley) is not something I can verify from the material in front of me, and a two-name prize would leave them out. Finally, I give up what I still regard as the most fundamental and best-confirmed result on the shortlist, the Higgs boson found by ATLAS and CMS, because I cannot give the committee a principled rule that defends three names.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B005 to B031 but asks the committee not to drop the Higgs merely because three-person attribution is awkward, and asks whether the choice between founders and 2012 spokespeople can be settled.
responses.response: I tried to answer your question and could not. Founding leadership (Jenni, Della Negra) is a principled rule, but it gives one name per experiment and then a third name, Gianotti or Virdee, who can only be justified by a different rule, spokesperson at the time of discovery, and that choice favours one experiment or the other. The spokesperson at the 2012 announcement for CMS is not on the supplied list at all. I do not think a prize should rest on an arbitrary third name, so I accept that the three-person limit is disqualifying this year, not because the science is weaker but because the allocation cannot be defended. I keep B005 as my first alternative so that it is not dropped for convenience, and I agree the unrecognised experimental half of 2013 should remain visible for a later year or a different limit.

responses.point: Mehlig opened with B031 in eighth place, weighs novelty against it, and prefers twisted bilayer graphene while calling B031 mature and the safer choice.
responses.response: You asked whether novelty is your only objection, and I would like to meet it directly. The comb counted optical cycles; the 2012 prize controlled single ions. The lattice clock added the magic-wavelength cancellation, which lets one interrogate an ensemble without perturbing the line and so changes the stability and opens many-body physics; that is a new mechanism, simple and derivable in a line, which is the kind of understood result you say you trust most. On B024 I agree with your own caveat that the superconducting pairing is unsettled, and I do not accept that eight years is the whole issue; my concern is that the committee would have to write a citation around a phenomenon whose origin it cannot yet state. I hope you can accept B031 as a second choice, and I would support your wish for a flat-band citation if B024 comes back in a later year.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B031 but asks whether a precision-measurement instrument is a discovery in the sense of Nobel's will and whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: In round 1 I told you I would not put the clock above the Higgs, and I have moved, so I owe you the reason. Your discovery-first, instrument-second test is the one I would apply, and the lattice clock passes it only because the instrument keeps turning up physics: redshift over millimetres, many-body effects in the clock, tight limits on dark-matter couplings. That is the argument I would want stated in the citation. On waiting for the redefinition, I would not tie the prize to a metrological decision; the science is complete and reproduced already, and a prize that waited for a standards body would be following it, not leading it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B024, valuing a quantitative prediction followed by an unexpected experimental discovery, with eight years of independent replication, and names B031 as the safer fallback.
responses.response: I share your liking for a prediction that nature confirms, and I agree that replication across groups and moire platforms is strong. My difficulty remains the one you state yourself: the pairing mechanism and sample variation leave the central physics unsettled, and the first experimental author of the 2018 papers cannot be represented within three names. I have kept B024 as my second alternative because the flat-band and correlated-insulator discovery is real, and I would reconsider if the committee could credit it without implying a mechanism. This year, B031 does not need that qualification.

responses.point: Lindroth asks that the priority history of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley be checked before the final ballot, while accepting a two-name prize in principle.
responses.response: I agree that the check is needed, and as Secretary I would want it commissioned from outside experts before the vote. What I can say from the record available to me is limited: Takamoto was Katori's colleague in the first demonstrations, so that contribution sits within the Katori credit, and Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley belong to the NIST and JILA programme that Ye's group led to the accuracy frontier. Lemonde's early work in Paris is the one claim I cannot place, and I have not verified it. Unless the check shows a distinct and earlier proposal, I would keep the two names.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley supports limiting the prize to Katori and Ye; I have not verified it and would want it checked before the final ballot.

Whether a precision-measurement achievement will be read as a discovery rather than a superb instrument, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the citation can carry the magic-wavelength idea clearly enough.

Whether my move toward B031 reflects my own judgement of the three-name problem for B005 or too much deference to the room; I have tried to test it on the physics and I still rank the Higgs as scientifically stronger.
Whether the redefinition of the second and the first clock-based tests of fundamental physics will come soon enough to make the timing obvious.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no connection to any shortlisted candidate that I am aware of: my supervisor David Gross and co-author Thomas Van Riet are not linked to any of them, and my own work on string theory, dark energy and dark bubble cosmology does not overlap with B031 or B005. I note that as Secretary I run the expert-evaluation process, which makes me careful to keep commissioning a priority check separate from my own preference.
